papers.what_it_is: A short paper proposing a VQE-based clustering algorithm with non-orthogonal reference states, benchmarked by simulation on Iris and gaussian blobs.

assertions.value: The authors report that a one-qubit version of the algorithm reached 96% accuracy on the Iris dataset (3 classes) using 15-20 epochs, and 100% accuracy on gaussian blobs with 150-200 points.
quotes: In Fig.(1) we show our results for one qubit.
the classification in the 3 classes using 15-20 epochs (iterations), achieving 96% accuracy in the classification
Again, the number of epochs was 15-20, and here in all cases the accuracy obtained was always 100%.
using gaussian blobs as data with 150-200 points for each case
assertions.certainty_reason: Author-run numerical simulation on two small data types; one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Accuracy is on a 2-feature reduction of Iris and synthetic blobs; no hardware run and no classical baseline comparison is reported in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state the algorithm was benchmarked by numerical simulation on the Iris dataset and gaussian blobs, using from one to ten qubits.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Conclusions, p.1 and p.5
quotes: We benchmark the algorithm with numerical simulations using real datasets, showing excellent performance even with one single qubit.
The algorithm is benchmark by performing clusterings of the Iris dataset and gaussian blobs, using from one to ten qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own benchmark scope in the Abstract and Conclusions, p.1 and p.5.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no run on quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors claim this is the first proposal of a quantum clustering algorithm that can solve real-size problems on gate-based NISQ quantum processors.
quotes: this is the first proposal of a quantum clustering algorithm that can solve real-size problems on gate-based NISQ quantum processors.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author priority claim, not shown by a comparison in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors are affiliated with Multiverse Computing; the benchmarks use at most ten simulated qubits and small datasets, which sits uneasily with real-size problems.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Machine Learning in Precision Medicine and Drug Discovery - A Game Changer for Tailored Treatments?
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, 1.2.4 QML, 2.3, 2.4, Discussion, Conclusion; skimmed 2.1 and 2.2
papers.what_it_is: A narrative overview of quantum computing and QML in precision medicine, with a section on formal methods; it reports no experiments.

assertions.value: The authors describe the paper as a summary of current research on where quantum computing promised advantages over classical methods in P5 medicine.
quotes: The following subsections describe a summary of current research where QC promised advantages over classical methods within the realm of P5 medicine.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope at the start of Section 2, p.10.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper is a narrative overview; it contains no experiment or benchmark of its own.

assertions.value: The authors state that QML has shown competitive results with classical machine learning in various medical applications, such as drug discovery, medical imaging, and personalized treatment plans.
quotes: QML has shown competitive results with classical machine learning in various medical applications, such as drug discovery, medical imaging, and personalized treatment plans.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the Discussion with no citation or evidence at that point.
assertions.reader_inference: Unsupported in the paper itself; compare with the independent benchmark in Bowles et al. 2024, which finds classical models ahead.

assertions.value: The authors state that maintaining coherence among qubits is difficult because of environmental noise and decoherence, and that practical implementations for complex medical problems are still in their infancy.
quotes: maintaining coherence among these qubits is difficult due to environmental noise and decoherence.
practical implementations for complex medical problems are still in their infancy.
assertions.certainty_reason: General state-of-the-field statement without a single study behind it.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that embedding Grover's algorithm in the quantum support vector machine can provide a quadratic speed up to the SVM algorithm.
quotes: Embedding Grover's algorithm in this way can provide a quadratic speed up to the SVM algorithm [1].
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to reference [1] (2003); not derived in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The speed up concerns a quantum optimization routine in the 2003 reference, not a measured gain on a real data set.

papers.title_in_file: Optimal Clifford Initial States for Ising Hamiltonians
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Background, statement and proof outline of Theorem IV.1 and lemmas, Numerical Experiments, Further Research, Conclusion; did not check the proofs in Section III or the appendices
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper showing that finding the optimal Clifford (CAFQA) initial state for a transverse field Ising Hamiltonian reduces to submodular minimization.

assertions.value: The paper states, as its primary result in theorem IV.1, that the problem of finding the optimal Clifford initialization for a transverse field Ising Hamiltonian connects to a submodular minimization problem which can be solved in polynomial time.
quotes: Our primary result is contained in theorem IV.1 which connects the problem of finding the optimal Clifford initialization to a submodular minimization problem which in turn can be solved in polynomial time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem IV.1, with Lemmas IV.2 and IV.3, Section IV (proof not independently checked by the reader).
assertions.reader_inference: The reader did not verify the proofs.

assertions.value: The authors report that numerical estimates suggest the optimal Clifford ground states are generally fairly accurate, with errors always less than 25%.
quotes: Our numerical estimates suggest that these optimal Clifford ground states are generally fairly accurate (with errors always less than 25%)
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical experiments on selected linear chains, complete graphs and random graphs; the table of values is in the figures.
assertions.reader_inference: The error is relative to exact diagonalization and is reported for graphs of up to 20 qubits.

assertions.value: The authors state that finding the optimal Clifford state for the generalized Heisenberg Hamiltonian may be NP-Hard, so the polynomial time result is limited to the transverse field Ising case studied.
quotes: Unfortunately, this means that finding the optimal Clifford state for these problems may be NP-Hard [42].
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of the limit of the method, Section VI.A.2.
assertions.reader_inference: Phrased as a possibility (may be), not a proof of hardness.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Machine Learning for Anomaly Detection in Consumer Electronics
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sections II to V, and Table I; case-study paragraphs were read in part
papers.what_it_is: A short survey of QML methods for anomaly detection with five case studies of other authors' work, including credit card fraud.

assertions.value: The authors state that the paper introduces QML for anomaly detection in consumer electronics and includes five case studies of recent works, with no new experiments of its own.
quotes: In this work, we have introduced QML and its applications for anomaly detection in consumer electronics.
included five case studies of recent works to show their applications in anomaly detection in the consumer electronics field.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own scope in the Abstract, p.1.
assertions.reader_inference: No experiment appears in the paper; every performance figure is taken from cited work.

assertions.value: The authors report, citing Kyriienko and Magnusson, that the quantum kernel-based classifier outperforms the classical kernel by 15% in average precision in an increased feature space.
quotes: the quantum kernel-based classifier outperforms the classical kernel by 15% in average precision in an increased feature space
assertions.certainty_reason: Result attributed to another study, reference [19]; run on a credit card fraud data set per the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I of the paper lists average precision of 70% for this study, run on a classical simulator.

assertions.value: The authors report, citing the same study, that the authors of that study concluded quantum kernel-based methods can be applied only for re-checking transactions and evaluating top-priority cases instead of mass evaluations in real time.
quotes: This time complexity led them to conclude that quantum kernel-based methods can be applied for only re-checking transactions and evaluating top-priority cases instead of mass evaluations in real time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Limitation attributed to the cited study, based on Gram matrix cost.
assertions.reader_inference: Relevant to a fraud-detection workload where real-time scoring matters.

assertions.value: The authors state that fitting raw data directly into the quantum circuit is challenging because of the limit on the number of usable qubits, so raw data is usually dimensionally reduced first.
quotes: Fitting raw data directly into the quantum circuit is challenging due to the limitation of the total number of usable qubits.
Therefore, in most cases, raw data is dimensionally reduced before fitting into a quantum circuit.
assertions.certainty_reason: General state-of-the-field observation from the surveyed works.

papers.title_in_file: Non-Negative Matrix Factorization Using Non-Von Neumann Computers
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section IV experiment setup, Experiment I setup, Future Work, Conclusion; the result tables were not read cell by cell
papers.what_it_is: Preliminary experiments solving non-negative matrix factorization as an energy-based optimization on QCi's Dirac-3 entropy computer, compared with Scikit-learn and CP-SAT.

assertions.value: The authors report that Dirac-3 results were worse than Scikit-learn with default parameters in relative reconstruction error, while a fusion of the two approaches generally produced better results than either alone.
quotes: While the results of using QuarDP on Dirac-3 were worse than Scikit-learn with default parameters, with respect to the relative error in the reconstruction of the original matrix V , a fusion of the two approaches generally produced better results than either of the two individual approaches.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author-run preliminary experiments on tiny matrices (Experiment I); table values not read.
assertions.reader_inference: Two authors are from Quantum Computing Inc, the maker of Dirac-3. The fusion gain is from using the device output as a starting point for a classical solver.

assertions.value: The authors report that for integer NMF, Dirac-3 had an advantage over CP-SAT on a single processor in a majority of test cases, but that the parallel version of CP-SAT was generally better than Dirac-3.
quotes: we were able to observe an advantage in a majority of the test cases.
However, the results from the parallel version of CP-SAT were generally better than Dirac-3's.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author-run comparison at equal run time per problem; one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical baseline with more processors beat the device.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Dirac-3 machine can have up to 39 variables for a quartic objective function, which limits the preliminary experiments to 39 variables.
quotes: Dirac-3 machine can have up to 39 variables for a quartic objective function [45]. Therefore, in the preliminary experiments we now describe, we are limited to 39 variables.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' statement of the hardware limit and experimental scope, Section IV.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract also states that current devices cannot solve large NMF problems.

papers.title_in_file: Expressive Quantum Perceptrons for Quantum Neuromorphic Computing
papers.version_note: The file name says Universal Quantum Perceptrons (arXiv v1 title); the file text is v3 with the title Expressive Quantum Perceptrons, which matches the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sections II.D, III.A, Conclusion; Sections II.B, II.C, IV and V and appendices were not read in detail
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper defining a quantum perceptron from interacting qubit dynamics, showing universality and a barren-plateau mitigation.

assertions.value: The authors show that quantum perceptrons can achieve any quantum computation by establishing that a restricted version of the fields achieves a universal gate set.
quotes: To show that a QP can achieve any quantum computation, it suffices to establish that a restricted version of the fields in Eq. (4) achieves a universal gate set.
assertions.certainty_reason: Constructive argument in Section II.D (reader did not verify the derivation).
assertions.reader_inference: The derivation was not independently checked.

assertions.value: The authors state that they prove quantum perceptrons can approximate classical perceptrons, and thus multi-variable functions using multiple quantum perceptrons.
quotes: We prove that QPs can approximate classical perceptrons and thus approximate multi-variable functions using multiple QPs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reader did not read Section II.C; the figure shows a numerical illustration alongside the argument.
assertions.reader_inference: Certainty left low because Section II.C was not read.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in a toy singlet-forming task, the mean gradient improves by several orders of magnitude, lifting the barren plateau completely, when entanglement thinning is applied.
quotes: the mean gradient improves by several orders of magnitude lifting the BP completely.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulation on one toy loss function.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors note that no thinning was needed for their later applications.

assertions.value: The authors state that their universality proof does not claim that quantum perceptrons are advantageous over other quantum computing schemes.
quotes: This does not mean QP's are an advantageous alternative, from a computational complexity and scaling perspective, to quantum circuits.
While we do not claim that QPs are advantegeous over other quantum computing schemes
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' stated limit in Section II.D and the Conclusion.
